pos: n. (the East Anglian county of Norwich, which received the Dutch and Walloon stranger churches in 1565 and bred the first English separatism)
etymology: Old English Norþfolc, the north folk of the East Angles, as against the Suþfolc to the south.
biblical_def: Norfolk is the northern half of East Anglia, and in the sixteenth century Norwich was the second city of England. Two things fix the county in the dictionary. In 1565 the city invited a company of Dutch and Walloon refugees, driven out of the Low Countries by the Spanish persecution, to settle and work the new draperies; by the fifteen-eighties they were some four or five thousand in a city of sixteen thousand, worshipping in their own tongues in the Blackfriars and in Bishop Herbert's chapel under their own elders and deacons and a discipline of their own. They were the plainest example in England of a Reformed church fully ordered, and the English Puritans watched them closely. Secondly, Robert Browne gathered at Norwich about 1581 the first avowedly separatist congregation in England, on the principle that a true church is a company of believers covenanting together without waiting for the magistrate; he fled to Middelburg, recanted, and left behind a name for the whole tendency. Kett's rebellion had gathered on Mousehold Heath in 1549 and ended in slaughter. The dictionary records Norfolk as the county where England saw a Reformed church at work, and marks what it refused to learn from it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stranger as a foreigner; a remnant as that which is left; an alien as one born in another country; a discipline as instruction and government; and a congregation as an assembly met for worship.
webster_full: STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown; a guest.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
ALIEN, n. A foreigner; one born in or belonging to another country; one not entitled to the privileges of a citizen.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
scriptures: Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
Isa 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Zep 3:12
I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD.
Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
corruption_summary: East Anglian county whose city of Norwich took in four or five thousand Dutch and Walloon refugees from 1565 and where Robert Browne gathered the first avowed separatist congregation about 1581.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's habitual method is a remnant, and that a remnant is usually poor and foreign-looking to the men among whom it is set. The strangers who came to Norwich were refugees with nothing but a trade and a church order; they were a quarter of the city within twenty years and they brought the new draperies with them. Paul states the doctrine as a present fact and not a consolation for bad times, that “at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5), and Isaiah says plainly what the alternative was, for “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9).

The second thing to recover is the character God assigns such a company, and it rules out both the contempt the strangers often met and the pride a settled church takes in sheltering them. Zephaniah describes what the LORD leaves behind after judgment: “I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:12). Our Lord names His own people in the same register, “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luk 12:32). As to Browne, the dictionary holds that his principle was right and his practice unstable: a church is indeed a company covenanting in Christ and does not wait on a magistrate's leave, and a man who argues that and then conforms under pressure has not disproved the argument, only discredited himself. The strangers' churches, which had order and elders and stayed put, were the better model.

pos: n. (the East Anglian county reckoned the most thoroughly preached in England, with a Puritan clothing district and a long roll of ejected ministers)
etymology: Old English Suþfolc, the south folk of the East Angles.
biblical_def: Suffolk is the southern half of East Anglia, and in the century between the Reformation and the Restoration it was probably the best-preached county in England. Its wealth came from cloth, and its clothing towns in the south and west, Lavenham, Sudbury, Hadleigh and Bury St Edmunds, were full of substantial independent men who wanted sermons and paid for them. Hadleigh under Rowland Taylor was a byword for a thoroughly reformed parish, and Taylor was burned on his own common in 1555. The county's ministers were numerous, learned and organised: Suffolk had its own conference in the Elizabethan period, and the county supplied Cambridge with students and New England with pastors in quantity. At the Restoration the county lost a very large number of its clergy, and its dissenting congregations were among the strongest in England thereafter. The dictionary records Suffolk as the plainest English demonstration of what happens where preaching is continuous for several generations in the same places, and it notes that the demonstration was paid for by weavers and clothiers who had no office in the church and simply wanted the Word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject; a sermon as such a discourse; a clothier as a maker of cloth; to publish as to make known; and glad tidings as good news.
webster_full: PREACH, v.i. To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of scripture.
SERMON, n. A discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman, for the purpose of religious instruction.
CLOTHIER, n. In English usage, a man who makes cloths; a maker of cloth.
PUBLISH, v.t. To discover or make known to mankind or to people in general what before was private or unknown.
TIDINGS, n. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
corruption_summary: Southern East Anglian county whose clothing towns paid for continuous preaching for several generations, whose Hadleigh under Rowland Taylor was a byword, and which lost a very large number of clergy in 1662.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching is a public and ordinary labour rather than an occasional performance, and that it works by accumulation. Suffolk is the evidence. Its towns had sermons on Sundays and weekday lectures besides, for generation after generation in the same streets, and at the end of that process the county had a population that could argue theology in a market and a ministry large enough that ejecting it in 1662 emptied scores of pulpits at once. Paul's charge to Timothy describes the manner exactly, and the manner is relentless: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2).

The second thing to recover is the reason God appointed so unimpressive an instrument, which is a doctrine about Himself and not a comment on technique. It pleased God “by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21), and the choice of so weak a means is deliberate. What the weak means carries is magnificent, and Scripture spends its best language on the messenger rather than the message-bearer's gifts: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace” (Isa 52:7). Paul quotes it in the chain that makes sending the hinge of the whole business, asking “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15). The Suffolk clothiers who endowed lectures were doing the sending, and the dictionary counts that among the most useful things English laymen ever did with money.

pos: n. (the English county north-east of London where Thomas Hooker's Chelmsford lectureship was suppressed in 1629 and from which the migration to New England was heaviest)
etymology: Old English East Seaxe, the East Saxons, the kingdom lying east of the Middle and West Saxons.
biblical_def: Essex is the county between the Thames and the Stour, and it had the double advantage of lying next to London and of being full of clothing towns. Lollardy survived there into the sixteenth century, and the Marian persecution fell heavily on the county, with burnings at Colchester and elsewhere. Its great episode is the suppression of the lectureships. In the sixteen-twenties Thomas Hooker was lecturer at Chelmsford, drawing hearers from the whole district and holding a weekly conference of ministers; in 1629 Laud, then bishop of London, moved against him, the lectureship was put down, and Hooker fled first to Holland and then to New England, where he founded Hartford. Forty-nine Essex ministers petitioned on his behalf and were refused. The county then sent emigrants in greater numbers than any other to Massachusetts, and its names were planted along the New England coast. The dictionary records the silencing as the proximate cause of the migration, and holds that a church which stops the mouths of its best preachers has not secured uniformity but exported its own strength.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lecture as a discourse read or pronounced on any subject; to silence as to put to silence; necessity as that which makes an act unavoidable; a bond as a fetter; and to constrain as to compel.
webster_full: LECTURE, n. A discourse read or pronounced on any subject; a discourse delivered for instruction in a church.
SILENCE, v.t. To oblige to hold the peace; to restrain from speaking; to put to silence; to forbid to preach.
NECESSITY, n. That which makes an act or event unavoidable; irresistible power or compulsion.
BOND, n. Any thing that binds; a cord, chain or fetter; in the plural, imprisonment, captivity.
CONSTRAIN, v.t. To compel or force; to urge with irresistible power; to confine by force.
scriptures: Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
Act 4:20
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
corruption_summary: County north-east of London, strong in Lollard survival and in cloth, where Laud suppressed Thomas Hooker's Chelmsford lectureship in 1629 and from which emigration to Massachusetts was heaviest.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the silencing of preachers by ecclesiastical authority, and the dictionary names Laud by name because the policy was his. Lectureships were endowed by townsmen precisely where the parish incumbent would not or could not preach; to put them down in the name of order was to prefer the appearance of uniformity to the feeding of the people, and the forty-nine ministers who petitioned for Hooker understood this perfectly. The thing cannot in fact be done to a man who is called. Jeremiah tried it on himself and failed, for he said “I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jer 20:9). Peter and John answered a court with the same impossibility, “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20).

The second paragraph states the consequence, which the dictionary presents as a judgment on the policy rather than an accident. Essex did not go quiet in 1629; Essex went to Massachusetts. A preacher under this necessity does not stop, he moves, and what Paul says of his own case holds for Hooker's: “necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!” (1Co 9:16). The attempt to bind the preacher leaves the Word unbound, as Paul observed from his own chain, “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). Laud secured Chelmsford and lost Connecticut, and the dictionary records that a bishop who silences a lecturer is not suppressing a faction but furnishing another country with a church.

pos: n. (the fenland county of Cambridge and Ely, whose university was the seminary of English Puritanism and of New England's ministry)
etymology: From Cambridge, Old English Grantabrycg, the bridge over the Granta, later altered to Cambridge; with scir, a shire.
biblical_def: Cambridgeshire is the fenland county holding the cathedral at Ely and the university at Cambridge, and in the dictionary it is the county of theological education. From the fifteen-twenties, when the men later called the Cambridge reformers met at the White Horse inn, through the long succession of Elizabethan and Jacobean divines, Cambridge was the nursery of English Reformed theology: William Perkins at Christ's and Great St Andrew's, Laurence Chaderton at Emmanuel, John Preston and Richard Sibbes, and a stream of men who went out to the parishes and to New England. Emmanuel College, founded in 1584 by Sir Walter Mildmay expressly to train preachers, sent so many men across the Atlantic that John Harvard, an Emmanuel graduate, gave his name and his library to the college in Massachusetts. The point of the place was never learning for its own sake; Mildmay told the queen he had set an acorn, and the acorn was a supply of preachers. The dictionary records the university as a means and not an end, and holds that a divinity school is justified by the pulpits it fills and by nothing else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a university as an assemblage of colleges; divinity as the science of divine things; a seminary as a place of education; doctrine as that which is taught; and to instruct as to teach.
webster_full: UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
DIVINITY, n. The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God and his relations to men; theology.
SEMINARY, n. The place or original stock whence anything is brought; a place of education; a school or academy.
DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; whatever is laid down as true by an instructor.
INSTRUCT, v.t. To teach; to inform the mind; to communicate knowledge; to direct; to enjoin.
scriptures: Ezr 7:10
For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
corruption_summary: Fenland county of Ely and Cambridge, whose university from the fifteen-twenties was the nursery of English Reformed theology and whose Emmanuel College was founded in 1584 expressly to train preachers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Ezra's order, which puts three things in a fixed sequence and will not let them be separated: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezr 7:10). Study, obedience, teaching, and in that order. A university that produces the first without the second breeds critics; one that attempts the third without the first breeds enthusiasts. Cambridge in its best period held all three together, and the proof is that its divines were pastors as well as authors.

The second thing to recover is the material a theological education works on, which is a given text and not a field of enquiry. Paul's charge is a short list of three public exercises and the first is simply reading: “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). The ground of the whole enterprise is the nature of the book, that “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16); a school that holds this will teach exposition, and one that does not will teach something else and call it divinity. Even the king of Israel was set to the same book daily, that “he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deu 17:19). Mildmay's acorn grew because it was planted in that soil, and the dictionary notes that Cambridge's later drift to Arianism and latitude came by way of the same colleges once the text ceased to govern them.

pos: n. (the Suffolk port whose town preacher Samuel Ward was silenced and imprisoned, and whose name was carried to Massachusetts)
etymology: Old English Gipeswic, the trading place at the gip or river mouth, from wic, a port or dwelling.
biblical_def: Ipswich is the county town and port of Suffolk, standing at the head of the Orwell, and one of the oldest continuously occupied English towns. Its place in the dictionary is its town preachership. Ipswich, like many corporate towns, paid a lecturer out of the borough purse, and from 1605 the post was held by Samuel Ward, a Cambridge man of great reputation and considerable nerve. He preached against the Spanish match and against the drift of policy in church and state, published a famous engraved satire in 1621, was proceeded against in the High Commission, deprived and imprisoned, and ended his days in the town after a spell in the Netherlands; he died in 1640. Many of his hearers emigrated, and the Massachusetts town of Ipswich was named for this one, with Nathaniel Ward, a kinsman, among the New England founders and the compiler of the Body of Liberties. The dictionary records the office of town preacher as a lawful and valuable thing, and records the proceedings against its holder as an abuse of ecclesiastical courts against a man whose only offence was plainness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a watchman as a sentinel; to warn as to give notice of danger; a housetop as the roof of a house; boldness as freedom from timidity; and to deprive as to divest of an office.
webster_full: WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch and give notice of danger or of the approach of an enemy.
WARN, v.t. To give notice of approaching or probable danger or evil; to caution against anything that may prove injurious.
HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house; among the Jews, a flat roof used as a place of resort.
BOLDNESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; freedom from timidity; liberty of speech.
DEPRIVE, v.t. To take from; to bereave of something possessed; to divest of an office or dignity.

So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.
Isa 62:6
I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,
What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
Phi 1:14
And many of the brethren in the Lord, waxing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
corruption_summary: Suffolk port whose town preacher Samuel Ward was proceeded against in the High Commission, deprived and imprisoned for plain preaching, and whose name was carried to Massachusetts.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of a church court to punish plainness, and the dictionary names the High Commission as the instrument. Ward was paid by the borough to preach to the town, and he preached about the things the town was anxious about; for that he was deprived and gaoled. The office he held is one Scripture describes in military terms and makes answerable to God rather than to a bishop: “I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7). A watchman who is forbidden to call out has not been disciplined; he has been disabled, and the fault is in the hand that silenced him. Isaiah expressly denies such men the option of quiet, charging them “which shall never hold their peace day nor night” (Isa 62:6).

The second paragraph names the method the Lord prescribes, which is publicity, and so condemns the policy twice over. The ministry is not conducted in private assurances to those who can be trusted with them: “What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops” (Mat 10:27). The outcome at Ipswich illustrates the futility as well as the wrong of the attempt. Ward in prison was more use to his people than Ward at liberty would have been to the Commission, and Paul describes the effect of his own confinement in terms that fit the town exactly: “many of the brethren in the Lord, waxing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear” (Phi 1:14). The men who sailed from the Orwell took the name of the town with them and set it on a new one.

pos: n. (the Essex clothing village whose classis of ministers met secretly from 1582 to 1589 as the first sustained presbyterian experiment in England)
etymology: Old English Dydda's ham, the homestead of Dydda; the Stour valley village in Essex.
biblical_def: Dedham is the Essex village on the Stour, rich from the cloth trade and crowned with a great perpendicular church tower built out of it. Its importance in the dictionary is wholly out of proportion to its size. From 1582 to 1589 a conference of some twenty ministers of the Stour valley on both sides of the river met at Dedham once a month, chiefly in the house of its minister, and kept minutes; the minutes survive and are the best evidence we have of how English Presbyterianism actually worked while it was illegal. They examined candidates, settled disputes between ministers and parishes, debated whether a man might read the prayers he disapproved, resolved cases of conscience about marriage and discipline, and corresponded with similar conferences elsewhere. There was no compulsion: a brother could decline the conference's advice, and sometimes did. The thing was broken up in 1589 when Whitgift's campaign against the classis movement reached Essex. The dictionary records the Dedham classis as the most instructive English precedent for presbyterian order, and marks that it was voluntary, local, minuted and entirely without civil power.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a classis as a body of ministers and elders; a conference as a meeting for consultation; fellowship as communion; a cord as a string or small rope; and a foundation as the basis of a building.
webster_full: CLASSIS, n. An assembly or body of ministers and elders; in some churches, a judicatory above the single congregation.
CONFERENCE, n. The act of conversing on a serious subject; a meeting of two or more persons for consultation.
FELLOWSHIP, n. Companionship; society; consort; mutual association on equal and friendly terms; communion.
CORD, n. A string, or small rope, composed of several strands twisted together.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that upon which anything stands, and by which it is supported.

And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Ecc 4:12
And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
corruption_summary: Essex clothing village on the Stour whose monthly conference of some twenty ministers met from 1582 to 1589 and left minutes, the best surviving evidence of English Presbyterianism in practice.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the association of churches is both lawful and voluntary, and that these two things do not contradict each other. The Dedham brethren met because they judged a minister ought not to decide hard cases alone; they kept minutes because a body that will not record its reasons cannot be held to them; and they claimed no coercive power, so that a brother might hear their advice and go his own way. That is association without prelacy. The apostolic church is described as continuing “stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42), where fellowship stands beside doctrine as a thing to be continued in rather than a sentiment to be felt.

The second thing to recover is the reason such a conference strengthens rather than dilutes a congregation. A village minister in the Stour valley in 1585 was isolated, watched and liable to be reported; twenty such men meeting monthly were a different proposition. Solomon's observation is about exactly this arithmetic: “if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12). The oneness of the first believers was practical and costly, for “the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32). And the whole structure rests where Paul puts it, on a foundation that no classis lays and none can move, since the church is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20). Whitgift broke the conference in 1589 and could not break what it had taught.

pos: n. (the Norfolk town that was the East Anglian see from 1072 until the bishop removed to Norwich in 1094, and the site of a great Cluniac priory)
etymology: Old English þeodford, the people's ford or the public ford, where the road crossed the Little Ouse.
biblical_def: Thetford is the Norfolk town at the confluence of the Thet and the Little Ouse, where the Icknield Way crossed the river. It was one of the chief towns of the Danelaw and briefly a cathedral city: Herfast moved the East Anglian see there from North Elmham in 1072, and Herbert de Losinga moved it again to Norwich in 1094, leaving Thetford with a Cluniac priory founded in 1103 that became the burial place of the Dukes of Norfolk. The priory held an image of Our Lady that drew pilgrims, and at the Dissolution the third Duke petitioned to keep the house as a college to preserve his family's tombs and was refused. The town declined; Thomas Paine was born there in 1737, the son of a Quaker staymaker. The dictionary's interest is in a see that moved and a priory that failed, and in the question they raise: what is it that the church is actually founded on, if not a site. A diocese may be carried ten miles up a river in a single decision, and nothing essential travels with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a see as the seat of episcopal power; a priory as a convent subordinate to an abbey; a corner stone as the stone uniting two walls; a rock as a large mass of stone; and to build as to construct an edifice.
webster_full: SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey.
CORNER STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone.
ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compacted and fixed in the earth; a defence; a firm support.
BUILD, v.t. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice or fabric; to raise by art; to establish.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
corruption_summary: Norfolk town at the crossing of the Icknield Way, the East Anglian see from 1072 until the bishop removed to Norwich in 1094, left with a Cluniac priory and a pilgrim image of Our Lady.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the reading of our Lord's word to Peter that makes a man and a place the foundation of the church, and Thetford is a convenient refutation of it. Here was a cathedral see for twenty-two years, and then it was somewhere else, and the church in Norfolk was neither created by the arrival nor destroyed by the departure. Christ's own promise is that “upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Mat 16:18), and the rock is the confession Peter had just made of Christ, not the office of a successor or the dignity of a city. Paul leaves no room for a second candidate: “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11).

The second paragraph names the other corruption that stayed behind when the bishop left, which is the image. The priory kept a figure of the Virgin that drew offerings and pilgrims, and the whole apparatus of lights, petitions and reported cures grew round it; the dictionary calls that idolatry and declines the distinction between veneration and worship by which it is defended. The stone the Scriptures direct men to is a person and is described as despised before it was honoured: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22). Isaiah gives the promise in the form of a foundation laid by God Himself, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16), and adds that the man who believes on it will not be in a hurry. A town that lost its see, its priory and its trade, and produced a staymaker's son who turned against the faith altogether, is a fair warning about building on anything else.

pos: n. (the Suffolk clothing town whose enormous church was built from broadcloth money, and which resisted the Amicable Grant in 1525)
etymology: Old English Lafanham, the homestead of Lafa; a Suffolk village in the Stour valley cloth country.
biblical_def: Lavenham is the Suffolk village that was for a time among the wealthiest towns in England, its money made from the blue broadcloth that the Suffolk weavers sold across Europe. The wealth is still legible: a church of cathedral proportions with a tower a hundred and forty feet high, built in the fourteen-eighties and nineties at the joint charge of the de Vere earls of Oxford and the Spring family of clothiers, whose merchant marks and chantry chapels are cut into the stonework. In 1525 Wolsey attempted the Amicable Grant, a forced loan without parliamentary sanction, and the Suffolk cloth towns refused it; several thousand men assembled at Lavenham, the clothiers having told their workers they could no longer employ them if the money were paid, and the Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk negotiated rather than fought. The grant was abandoned. The trade declined in the next century as the new draperies took the market. The dictionary records the church and the chantries together, and asks the question the building itself raises about religion paid for out of surplus and built to commemorate the payer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chantry as an endowment for the saying of masses; broadcloth as a fine woollen cloth; a sepulchre as a burial place; outward as external; and hypocrisy as the assuming of a false appearance of virtue.
webster_full: CHANTRY, n. A church or chapel endowed with lands for the maintenance of priests to sing mass for the souls of the donors.
BROADCLOTH, n. A species of woollen cloth, so called from its breadth.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
OUTWARD, a. External; exterior; forming the superficial part; adventitious; not intrinsic.
HYPOCRISY, n. Simulation; a feigning to be what one is not; the assuming of a false appearance of virtue or religion.
scriptures: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
Isa 1:11

To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats.
Hos 6:6
For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
Rev 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
corruption_summary: Suffolk cloth village whose church of cathedral proportions was built in the fourteen-eighties by the de Veres and the Spring clothiers, and which refused Wolsey's Amicable Grant in 1525.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the chantry, and Lavenham is where an Englishman can still see it carved into a wall. A chantry was an endowment to pay a priest to say masses for the soul of the founder, and the Spring family bought chapels, marks and prayers in the church their money built; the whole system assumed that the dead may be helped by purchased offices and that a man's estate may buy him a shorter purgatory. The dictionary names that as a denial of the finished work of Christ and a trade in what cannot be sold. The Lord's word about religion that is magnificent outside is the word for the building and the arrangement both: “ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones” (Mat 23:27).

The second paragraph puts the general rule, because the dictionary does not object to a fine church. God's complaint through Isaiah is never against quantity but against substitution, asking “To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me?” (Isa 1:11) of a people whose offerings were many and whose obedience was not. Hosea states the preference in one line, “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos 6:6). And the danger of a prosperous town is the danger of Laodicea, told it did not know its own condition: “thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor” (Rev 3:17). Lavenham refused an illegal tax in 1525 and lost its trade within a century; the tower is still there, and the dictionary holds that the tower was the smaller of the two things the broadcloth bought, the larger being a parish that learned to read.

pos: n. (the Suffolk castle of the Howards where Mary Tudor was proclaimed queen in July 1553)
etymology: Old English Framelingaham, the homestead of Framela's people.
biblical_def: Framlingham is the Suffolk market town whose castle, a curtain wall with thirteen towers and no keep, was the seat of the Howard dukes of Norfolk. Its one day of national importance is in July 1553. Edward VI died on the sixth; Northumberland proclaimed Lady Jane Grey; Mary, who had been at Kenninghall, withdrew to Framlingham as the strongest place she could reach and gathered her supporters in the park below the walls. The East Anglian gentry came in, the fleet in Yarmouth roads declared for her, the council in London changed sides, and on the nineteenth she was proclaimed in the City; she rode from Framlingham to London and to a reign in which some three hundred people were burned. The Howards, who had kept the old religion, were restored. The dictionary records the accession as a providence and refuses to make the providence a verdict. That God brought Mary to the throne from a Suffolk castle is certain; that the burnings which followed were therefore approved is not, and the dictionary insists on the distinction because it is the distinction every party in that century got wrong about its own successes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines providence as the care and superintendence of God; a lot as that which falls by chance; succession as the order of coming into an office; to proclaim as to publish by authority; and a chariot as a car of war.
webster_full: PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a manifestation of the care of God.
LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance; the decision of chance or divine providence by casting lots.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; the order of coming into a throne or office after another.
PROCLAIM, v.t. To promulgate; to announce; to publish by authority, as a king or a herald.
CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a carriage with four wheels; a car of war used by the ancients in battle.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Suffolk castle of the Howard dukes where Mary Tudor withdrew in July 1553 and was proclaimed queen, going from it to London and to a reign in which some three hundred were burned.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the argument from success, and the dictionary names it as an error committed by every side in the Tudor century. Mary's partisans read her bloodless accession as heaven's endorsement of the old religion and proceeded to the fires; her opponents, when Elizabeth came in, read that as heaven's endorsement of theirs. Both reasoned from an event to a doctrine, which Scripture never permits. That the outcome was God's doing is not in dispute, for “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33); what the outcome does not do is tell anyone what to believe. The rule of faith is the Word, and a providence is not a revelation.

The second paragraph names the practical error that follows, which is the transfer of hope to a person or a party. Framlingham in July 1553 was full of gentlemen calculating which claimant would reward them, and the fleet changed sides on the same arithmetic. The psalmist forbids the whole exercise: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3), and sets the contrast plainly, “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Solomon grants the duty of preparation and locates the outcome elsewhere, since “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). Mary rode out of a Suffolk park to a crown and to five years; the men who had come in to her park got very little by it, and the three hundred who were burned under her are the dictionary's reason for naming the lesson sharply.

pos: n. (the Norfolk village whose shrine of Our Lady was the chief English pilgrimage after Canterbury until it was destroyed in 1538)
etymology: Old English Walsingaham, the homestead of Wals's people; a Norfolk village near the north coast.
biblical_def: Walsingham is the north Norfolk village which held, from the eleventh century until 1538, the greatest Marian shrine in England. The foundation legend is that a noblewoman named Richeldis was shown the house of the Annunciation in a vision about 1061 and built a replica, the Holy House, at Walsingham; an Augustinian priory grew round it. By the later Middle Ages it was the second pilgrimage of the kingdom after Becket's tomb, with a Slipper Chapel a mile out where pilgrims left their shoes to walk the last stretch barefoot, a relic of the Virgin's milk among its treasures, and kings from Henry III to Henry VIII among its visitors; Erasmus went and wrote a satirical account of what he was shown. In 1538 the image was taken to Chelsea and burned and the priory was suppressed. The shrine was revived in 1922 by an Anglo-Catholic vicar and a Roman shrine was established at the Slipper Chapel, and both now draw large pilgrimages. The dictionary names the whole business as idolatry, the more plainly because it has been restored in living memory and is now defended as heritage.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines idolatry as the worship of images; a relic as the remains of a saint; to invoke as to address in prayer; a cistern as a receptacle for water; and separate as divided from the rest.
webster_full: IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images or anything made by hands, or which is not God.
RELIC, n. That which remains; the body of a deceased person, or some part of it; remains preserved with veneration.
INVOKE, v.t. To address in prayer; to call on for assistance and protection.
CISTERN, n. An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor.
SEPARATE, a. Divided from the rest; being parted from another; disunited; disconnected.
scriptures: Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
corruption_summary: North Norfolk village whose Holy House and shrine of Our Lady was the chief English pilgrimage after Canterbury until the image was burned in 1538, and which was revived in 1922.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not a subtlety requiring excavation; it is a shrine, and the dictionary names it as idolatry in the plain sense of the second commandment. An image was set up, prayers were addressed to the person it represented, a relic of the Virgin's milk was displayed, pilgrims walked the last mile barefoot and paid, and a priory lived on the proceeds for four and a half centuries. The commandment forbids the making and the bowing both: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). Paul's instruction to a church in a city full of such places is one word and a direction of travel, “flee from idolatry” (1Co 10:14). The distinction between the veneration of an image and the worship of it was invented to answer this text and does not answer it.

The second paragraph is the modern half, and it is why the entry is sharp. The shrine was destroyed in 1538 and rebuilt in 1922, and it is now defended not chiefly on doctrinal grounds but as English heritage, a place of quiet, a continuity with the medieval past. The dictionary declines that defence entirely. A thing forbidden is not permitted by age, and the reason men turn to such places is the one Jeremiah gives, that they have left a spring for a tank that leaks: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). The command to those who see it for what it is remains a command to leave: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing” (2Co 6:17). That a pilgrimage is well attended is not an argument; Walsingham was well attended in 1500 too.
